item.title: Encounter One — The Slowing of the Room
item.description:
This encounter first appears as a familiar reflective problem: a transition did not work, and the teacher later identifies pacing as the issue. Through Kolb, Gibbs, or Schön, the event could be organized as observation, evaluation, and future adjustment. Yet in Tauira this encounter should not remain a closed lesson about technique.

Rhizomatically, the event links to recurring nodes across the project: analytic performance, material orientation, visible evidence, and the production of compliance. The encounter therefore matters less as a single failure of pacing than as one expression of a wider pattern in which pedagogical rigour, classroom objects, and evaluative pressure repeatedly thin relation. See also [[enc-2025-T1-W5-L3]] for the recurrence of legitimacy and form, and [[memo-001]] for the map of compliance-affect across encounters.

item.title: Encounter Two — The Homework that Changed Shape
item.description:
This encounter can easily be narrated in reflective discourse as a successful act of differentiation. Kolb, Gibbs, and Schön all support that reading by helping the teacher convert the event into professional learning about flexibility. In Tauira, however, the event should remain open as a site where medium, legitimacy, and authority are redistributed.

Rhizomatically, this encounter connects to other nodes beyond differentiation: written legitimacy, assessment comfort, visible rigour, and the politics of medium. It is therefore not only about one student and one task. It belongs to a wider network in which writing repeatedly appears as the default carrier of seriousness, while alternative media expose the material-discursive preferences through which teacher authority is stabilised. See [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] for the recurrence of visible evidence, and [[memo-002]] for the cross-encounter map of legitimacy, medium, and comfort.

item.title: Encounter Three — The Sadness in the Room
item.description:
This encounter can be processed through familiar reflective theories as an instance of sensitive facilitation, reflection-in-action, or later professional learning about care. Those readings remain useful. But Tauira should hold the event as more than a lesson in better handling difficult topics.

Rhizomatically, this encounter links concept to affect, affect to temporality, and temporality to role instability. It therefore extends beyond the individual student response and becomes part of a wider map of how knowledge enters bodies, memories, and ethical relations. In this network, sadness is not outside learning. It is one of the ways the pedagogical assemblage makes learning happen. See [[enc-2025-T1-W3-L2]] for the recurrence of affective shifts in the room, and [[memo-003]] for the threshold map connecting concept, identity, and pedagogical tempo.
